primary_topics: Institute of Corporate Directors Breakfast Roundtable address, September 28, 2011 -- six-topic analysis of the nature, duties, independence safeguards, SEC improper impositions, and available remedies for Independent Directors

The SEC's proposed 5-5 plan: limit IDs to five consecutive years in one corporation and not more than five publicly listed corporations simultaneously -- CJP argues these are not in the SRC but are 'SEC-originated inventions and impositions' beyond its legal mandate

The constitutional independence analogy: 'Can SC justices who are appointed yearly by the President and whose compensation is dependent totally on Congress be expected to be independent?' If SC justices can maintain independence without tenure protection, the SEC's argument for restricting IDs to achieve independence fails
Four remedies for those affected by improper SEC regulations: persuasion, administrative route, judicial route (showing SEC exceeded its authority), and Ombudsman complaints against SEC officials
sub_topics: Nature of Independent Directorship: must own at least one share; elected per Corporation Code; all directors are trustees or fiduciaries; must uphold welfare and interests of corporation above private interests; collectively exercise corporate powers, conduct business and control property; IDs get no additional compensation beyond director fees (unlike executive directors)

SRC Section 38 definition: 'a person other than an officer or employee of the corporation, its parent or subsidiaries, or any other individual having a relationship with the corporation, which would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment'

Distinctive duty: worded like the Ten Commandments (negative covenants); ID must be independent of management; expected to 'fiscalize and counter-check management and even the controlling shareholders who elected him'; uphold laws, articles and bylaws, corporate ethics canons, corporate governance manual; must be 'sufficiently courageous and independent' to oppose management if necessary

Safeguarding independence: unlike judges, IDs have no constitutional security of tenure or compensation; 'an Independent Director will only become such if he is acceptable to the board majority and the controlling shareholders'; term of one year; continuation depends on controlling shareholders

SEC 5-5 plan critique: five consecutive years in one corporation; not more than five publicly listed corporations simultaneously; 'like the Ten Commandments and the SRC, these prohibitions are NOT provided in the SRC but are SEC-originated inventions and impositions'; SC justices analogy -- 'by the same token, can we truly expect full independence from IDs who depend on the votes of the majority to be elected yearly?'; 'instead of restricting the prerogatives of IDs, the first order of the day should be to strengthen their independence and integrity'

Four remedies: (1) persuasion; (2) administrative route; (3) judicial route -- 'show that the SEC abused and exceeded its power and authority'; (4) sue the SEC officials in the Office of the Ombudsman
Closing principle: 'the end never justifies the means. However laudable its motives, the SEC must not impose unreasonable, whimsical and illegal inventions beyond its legal mandate'

stances.claim: The SEC's 5-5 plan (five consecutive years per corporation; maximum five PLCs simultaneously) is legally infirm: it imposes restrictions NOT found in the SRC -- which defines IDs in Section 38 but does not limit their tenure or number of seats. Only Congress can impose such restrictions through legislation, not the SEC through administrative regulation. The end (improving corporate governance) does not justify these ultra-vires means.
stances.rhetorical_move: ultra-vires argument: the SEC 5-5 plan as an administrative invention beyond the statutory grant -- the Ten Commandments analogy making the negative-covenant structure of Section 38 clear
stances.confidence: asserted as a firm legal position

stances.claim: Restricting ID tenure and board seats is counterproductive: if the goal is to produce independent directors, the solution is to strengthen their independence and integrity, not to limit the experienced ones. SC justices -- appointed annually by the President, with compensation fully dependent on Congress -- manage to be independent. IDs, who at least get elected by shareholders, can too if properly supported.
stances.rhetorical_move: SC-justice-independence-analogy: judicial independence achieved without the SEC's proposed restrictions as proof that ID independence can be achieved without them

notable_anecdotes: The Ten Commandments analogy for Section 38: the SRC's definition of IDs, like the Ten Commandments, is worded as negative covenants ('a person OTHER than an officer or employee... having a relationship... which would interfere'); just as the Ten Commandments say 'Thou shalt not,' the SRC says 'not this, not that' -- and the 5-5 plan adds prohibitions that are not in the original text.

The SC justice analogy: 'Can Supreme Court justices who are appointed yearly by the President and whose compensation is dependent totally on Congress be expected to be independent? By the same token, can we truly expect full independence from IDs who depend on the votes of the majority to be elected yearly?' -- the institutional analogy that exposes the SEC's flawed reasoning.

Four remedies enumerated: (1) persuasion (professional engagement with SEC); (2) administrative route (formal SEC processes); (3) judicial route (showing SEC exceeded its authority); (4) Ombudsman complaints against SEC officials. A progressively escalating set of options for those harmed by the 5-5 plan.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 28, 2011 at the Institute of Corporate Directors Breakfast Roundtable -- invited by Chairman Dr. Jesus P. Estanislao -- this six-topic address by CJP analyzes the nature, duties, independence safeguards, SEC propositions and remedies for Independent Directors. An ID must own at least one share, be elected per the Corporation Code, serve as a trustee/fiduciary of the corporation above private interests, and receive no additional compensation beyond director fees. SRC Section 38 defines IDs through negative covenants ('other than an officer or employee... having a relationship... which would interfere with independent judgment') -- 'worded like the Ten Commandments.' The ID's distinctive duty: fiscalize and counter-check management and controlling shareholders; uphold laws, articles, bylaws, ethics canons and governance manuals; be 'sufficiently courageous and independent' to oppose management when necessary. Unlike judges, IDs have no constitutional security of tenure or compensation -- their continuation depends on controlling shareholders. On the SEC's proposed 5-5 plan (five consecutive years per corporation; maximum five PLCs simultaneously): 'like the Ten Commandments and the SRC, these prohibitions are NOT provided in the SRC but are SEC-originated inventions and impositions.' The SC justice analogy: 'Can SC justices appointed annually by the President and whose compensation depends totally on Congress be expected to be independent? By the same token, can we truly expect full independence from IDs who depend on the votes of the majority?' The solution: 'instead of restricting the prerogatives of IDs, the first order of the day should be to strengthen their independence and integrity so they can perform their lonely work effectively.' Four remedies: persuasion, administrative route, judicial route (showing SEC exceeded its authority), and Ombudsman complaints against SEC officials. Close: 'the end never justifies the means. However laudable its motives, the SEC must not impose unreasonable, whimsical and illegal inventions beyond its legal mandate.'
